title: Sensitivity of air pollution in eastern Canada to regional emissions and meteorology Part 2: PM 2.5
content: Particulate matter with aerodynamic diameter ≤ 2.5 µm (PM2.5) can remain aloft for days, crossing political boundaries and adversely affecting human health in other jurisdictions than those where it was emitted. Because its formation, transport, and removal depend on meteorological conditions, climate change may alter both PM2.5 concentrations and their sensitivity to regional emissions. Based on GEOS-Chem chemical transport model output, we created monthly statistical emulators to capture the effects of meteorology on PM2.5 concentrations over eastern Canada. We then drove the emulators with CRCM5 regional climate model output to project how climate change will affect PM2.5 concentrations. We project domain-mean climate-driven PM2.5 increases of approximately 0.54 µg m−3 under RCP4.5 and 1.15 µg m−3 under RCP8.5. We additionally created emulators based on simulations with anthropogenic emissions zeroed out in three regions: Quebec, the rest of Canada, and the US. We used these to project how climate change may affect the contributions of anthropogenic emissions from each of these regions to PM2.5 concentrations. We project that climate change will increase the US contribution to PM2.5 more than the Canadian and Québécois contributions. Changes in 850-hPa wind components do not explain the spatial pattern. Instead, increased temperatures enhance the PM2.5 formation efficiency, thus enhancing pre-existing disparities in anthropogenic PM2.5 precursor emissions from each region. If this is robust to other regions, it suggests that climate change may exacerbate pollution export across political boundaries.
